title: Rochdale mum Jen Daker swaps classroom for personal training — and finds the best shape of her life
body:
For 16 years, Jen Daker knew exactly where she belonged: in education, working with children at the same school she had called her professional home for most of her adult life. Then motherhood changed the shape of her priorities — and fitness changed the direction of her career.

Now 36, a mum of two and a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, Jen has taken the discipline she built in the gym and turned it into a second career helping other women and men become stronger, healthier and, perhaps most importantly, more confident.

It was not a rejection of her old life. Jen says she loved working in education and with children. But after two pregnancies, training became far more than a way to look fit. It helped her regain physical strength, improved her mental wellbeing and gave her a precious sense of herself outside the daily demands of work and motherhood.

That experience planted the idea of becoming a personal trainer. If exercise could make her feel that different, she reasoned, perhaps she could help other people find the same thing.

Leaving the security of a 16-year career at 36, with two young children and a mortgage, took courage. Jen is equally clear that courage was not hers alone. Her partner Damien has been central to making the change possible, sharing the load through the early mornings, late evenings and weekends that come with building a new career around family life.

“Having someone who believes in you, encourages you and helps share the load makes such a difference,” Jen said. “My family have been my biggest supporters from day one.”

That support matters because Jen's discipline starts early. On mornings after broken sleep with the children, staying in bed can be tempting. But she sees her first workout of the day as more than exercise. Before the school runs, clients, work and everything else that comes with being a mum, it is an hour that belongs to her.

Training first thing, she says, sets the tone for the day. She has more energy, feels brighter and has already done something positive for herself before everybody else needs something from her. It is a lesson she wants other mothers to hear because, as she puts it, mums can become very good at putting themselves last.

The striking thing about Jen's approach is that the discipline is strong without becoming rigid. She does not pretend to wake up overflowing with motivation every morning. “Motivation comes and goes, but habits keep you going,” she said. Some sessions are brilliant and some are not. Showing up is what matters.

Exercise is now as important to Jen's head as it is to her body. She describes herself as someone with a very active brain who can struggle to switch off. Training gives her headspace, a reset button amid the noise of work and family life, and has helped build both confidence and resilience.

She no longer trains simply because she wants to look a certain way. She trains because she knows how much better movement makes her feel mentally.

But that does not mean every difficult day should be answered with a punishing gym session. Jen admits this is something she is still learning herself. There are days when exhaustion or overwhelm mean a walk, some stretching or proper rest is the healthier choice. “Fitness should support your wellbeing, not become another source of pressure,” she said.

The same realism runs through her approach to food. Jen loves food and does not believe a sustainable healthy life should be built around guilt, deprivation or a list of things that are permanently off limits. One meal or one night out cannot erase months of healthy habits, just as one salad cannot suddenly make somebody healthy.

Her message to clients is simple: life is for living. Enjoy birthdays. Go on holiday. Make memories. Eat the foods you love in moderation and then return to your normal routine without treating enjoyment as failure.

“Consistency wins every time,” Jen said. “It's what you do most of the time that matters, not what you do occasionally.”

That philosophy also shapes how she speaks to people who feel they have fallen off track. There is no need to wait for Monday, a new month or the perfect burst of motivation. One walk, one healthier meal or one short gym session is enough to restart. Small actions, repeated, become a lifestyle.

For Jen, the most rewarding evidence of that philosophy is not always visible in a before-and-after photograph. One of her first clients found her through a Facebook recommendation. The woman had never been to a gym, was nervous and lacked confidence. Over time, she began to believe in herself. While Jen was away on holiday, the client even went to the gym alone — something she once could not imagine doing.

Jen says she barely recognises the hesitant person she first met. The transformation has reached far beyond exercise. “The biggest transformation isn't always physical — it's the confidence people gain in every part of their lives,” she said.

She sees that particularly among mothers who can feel they have “lost” themselves somewhere inside motherhood. Helping somebody recover a sense of capability and identity is, for Jen, one of the best parts of the job.

She is also keen to puncture the idea that personal trainers stride around the gym permanently confident in themselves. In fact, she believes working every day in a fitness environment can make trainers pick themselves apart if they let it. Nor do good trainers expect a new client to arrive already fit. Their job is to help somebody improve from the place they are actually starting.

Jen still gets gym nerves herself. After returning from a recent two-week holiday, even she felt apprehensive about her first session back. Her reassurance for beginners is straightforward: nearly everybody feels nervous the first time, most people in the gym are concentrating on their own workout, and every confident person in the room was once a beginner. The hardest part is often simply walking through the door.

Behind the training schedule is a family life Jen plainly treasures. She does not claim to have discovered some flawless formula for balancing children, a relationship, work, fitness and time for herself. Social media, she points out, is a highlight reel. Some weeks work better than others. A workout, a walk or even a quiet coffee can be enough to give her the breathing room she needs to be a better mum, partner and PT.

That makes Jen's story more compelling than a picture of perfect balance. The old cliché says women cannot “have it all”. Her example suggests a more useful answer: nobody gets every part of life perfectly balanced every day, but with discipline, realistic expectations and a rock-solid support system, it is possible to get remarkably close.

Jen has not chosen between loving her children, protecting her relationship with Damien, pursuing an ambitious new career and looking after herself. Instead, the family have worked together to make room for all of it. The result is a woman in the strongest chapter of her life, physically and professionally, without pretending that strength means perfection.

The Hybrid Hut has become the professional home for that next chapter. Jen describes the Rochdale gym as a place where age, experience and starting fitness level do not determine whether somebody belongs. Beginners, experienced athletes, younger people and older clients are all welcome.

She now offers one-to-one personal training, small-group sessions and tailored online fitness plans for people of different ages and abilities, with one goal running through everything she does: make fitness feel welcoming, enjoyable and achievable in real life.

There is a neat continuity in the career change. Jen may have left the classroom after 16 years, but she has not stopped teaching. She is still encouraging people, still building confidence and still helping others discover what they are capable of. Only now, the classroom has a squat rack.

People interested in training with Jen can find her on Instagram or Facebook, or visit The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale.
excerpt: After 16 years in education, mum-of-two Jen Daker has found a new calling as a personal trainer at The Hybrid Hut in Rochdale, helping others build strength, confidence and healthier habits.
